inputs.dissolutionReason: Winding down operations following the sale of substantially all company assets

expectedText:
CORPORATE DISSOLUTION (CERTIFICATE OF DISSOLUTION)
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

RECITALS — CORPORATE DISSOLUTION AND WINDING UP
Acme, Inc. elected to voluntarily wind up and dissolve effective December 31, 2026, based on Winding down operations following the sale of substantially all company assets. This document records the winding up of Acme, Inc.'s affairs and the certificate of dissolution that formally ends Acme, Inc.'s corporate powers, rights, and privileges with the California Secretary of State. It addresses the statutory winding-up and dissolution process itself — a separate matter from whatever dissolution triggers or approval procedures appear in Acme, Inc.'s own bylaws or shareholder agreements, which govern only when and how the decision to dissolve is made internally, not how the corporation's existence is actually wound up and ended with the state.

GROUNDS FOR VOLUNTARY DISSOLUTION
California law lets a corporation elect to voluntarily wind up and dissolve in two distinct ways. First, any corporation may make that election by the vote of shareholders holding shares representing 50 percent or more of the voting power — a single, fixed threshold. Second, a narrower election path is available to the board alone, without any shareholder vote, but only for a corporation that falls into one of three specific categories: one as to which a federal bankruptcy court has entered an order for relief under Chapter 7; one that has disposed of all its assets and has not conducted any business for the five years immediately preceding the board's resolution to dissolve; or one that has issued no shares at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any corporation may elect voluntarily to wind up and dissolve by the vote of shareholders holding shares representing 50 percent or more of the voting power."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1900(a), General Corporation Law, voluntary dissolution by shareholder vote (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1900.)
  "Any corporation which comes within one of the following descriptions may elect by approval by the board to wind up and dissolve:(1) A corporation as to which an order for relief has been entered under Chapter 7 of the federal bankruptcy law.(2) A corporation which has disposed of all of its assets and has not conducted any business for a period of five years immediately preceding the adoption of the resolution electing to dissolve the corporation.(3) A corporation which has issued no shares."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1900(b), General Corporation Law, the narrower board-only election path (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1900.)
  Known gap: This corrects an assumption this research started with: Corporations Code section 1900 sets a fixed 50-percent-or-more shareholder-vote threshold for the general voluntary-dissolution election, and its text includes no 'or as otherwise specified in the articles' qualifier letting the articles of incorporation raise, lower, or otherwise vary that threshold — unlike some other California entity-dissolution statutes (including the LLC dissolution statutes addressed in a separate document in this project), section 1900 does not defer to the corporation's own governing documents on this point. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different vote thresholds. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1900, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

COMMENCEMENT OF WINDING UP AND THE BOARD'S POWERS
Voluntary winding-up proceedings for a corporation commence upon the adoption of the shareholders' or directors' resolution electing to wind up and dissolve, or upon the filing with the corporation of a written consent of shareholders to that effect. Once that happens, the corporation must stop carrying on business except so far as necessary to wind up beneficially, or during whatever period the board considers necessary to preserve the corporation's goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of its business or assets. The board must give written notice by mail of the start of the winding-up proceeding to all shareholders — except shareholders who voted in favor of the dissolution — and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the corporation's own records. The board continues to act as the board throughout, both before and after the certificate of dissolution is filed, and state law gives the directors and officers a specific, non-exclusive list of powers to exercise in the corporation's name for winding up: electing officers and employing agents and attorneys to liquidate the corporation's affairs; continuing the business only so far as necessary for its disposal or winding up; carrying out contracts and collecting, paying, compromising, and settling debts and claims for or against the corporation; defending suits brought against the corporation; suing in the corporation's name for amounts owed to it or to recover its property; collecting unpaid share subscriptions or recovering unlawful distributions; selling, exchanging, conveying, or otherwise disposing of corporate assets on terms the board deems reasonable; and, generally, making contracts and doing anything in the corporation's name that is proper or convenient for winding up, settling, and liquidating its affairs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Voluntary proceedings for winding up the corporation commence upon the adoption of the resolution of shareholders or directors of the corporation electing to wind up and dissolve, or upon the filing with the corporation of a written consent of shareholders thereto.(b) When a voluntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the board shall continue to act as a board and shall have full powers to wind up and settle its affairs, both before and after the filing of the certificate of dissolution.(c) When a voluntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the corporation shall cease to carry on business except to the extent necessary for the beneficial winding up thereof and except during such period as the board may deem necessary to preserve the corporation’s goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of its business or assets, or both, in whole or in part. The board shall cause written notice of the commencement of the proceeding for voluntary winding up to be given by mail to all shareholders (except no notice need be given to the shareholders who voted in favor of winding up and dissolving the corporation) and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the records of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1903, General Corporation Law, commencement of voluntary winding up and notice to shareholders and creditors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1903.)
  "The powers and duties of the directors (or other persons appointed by the court pursuant to Section 1805) and officers after commencement of a dissolution proceeding include, but are not limited to, the following acts in the name and on behalf of the corporation:(a) To elect officers and to employ agents and attorneys to liquidate or wind up its affairs.(b) To continue the conduct of the business insofar as necessary for the disposal or winding up thereof.(c) To carry out contracts and collect, pay, compromise and settle debts and claims for or against the corporation.(d) To defend suits brought against the corporation.(e) To sue, in the name of the corporation, for all sums due or owing to the corporation or to recover any of its property.(f) To collect any amounts remaining unpaid on subscriptions to shares or to recover unlawful distributions.(g) To sell at public or private sale, exchange, convey or otherwise dispose of all or any part of the assets of the corporation for cash in an amount deemed reasonable by the board without compliance with the provisions of Section 1001 (except subdivision (d) thereof), or (subject to compliance with the provisions of Sections 1001, 1200 and 1201, but Chapter 13 (commencing with Section 1300) shall not be applicable thereto) upon such other terms and conditions and for such other considerations as the board deems reasonable or expedient; and to execute bills of sale and deeds of conveyance in the name of the corporation.(h) In general, to make contracts and to do any and all things in the name of the corporation which may be proper or convenient for the purposes of winding up, settling and liquidating the affairs of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2001, General Corporation Law, the directors' and officers' powers during winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2001.)

This clause also corrects an assumption this research started with: the concrete list of winding-up activities (collecting assets, disposing of property not to be distributed in kind, discharging or providing for liabilities, and so on) is not found in Cal. Corp. Code § 1903, which instead addresses only when winding up commences, when the corporation must stop ordinary business, and what notice the board must give; the actual statutory list of the directors' and officers' winding-up powers and activities is codified separately, at Cal. Corp. Code § 2001. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections (§ 1903 and § 2001), not subsections of a single section.

THE CERTIFICATE OF ELECTION AND THE CERTIFICATE OF DISSOLUTION
Formally dissolving a California corporation generally involves a certificate evidencing the election to wind up and dissolve, filed once that election is made, and a separate certificate of dissolution filed later, once winding up is complete. The certificate of election must be an officers' certificate, or be signed and verified by a majority of the sitting directors, or by shareholders authorized to sign it by holders of 50 percent or more of the voting power, and it must state that the corporation elected to dissolve along with details of how that election was made. If the election was made by the vote of all the outstanding shares — not merely 50 percent or more — and the later certificate of dissolution itself states that the election was made by all outstanding shares, the separate certificate of election does not need to be filed at all. The certificate of dissolution itself, once winding up is complete, is signed and verified by a majority of the sitting directors and states that the corporation has been completely wound up, how its known debts and liabilities were handled, that its known assets have been distributed (or that none were acquired), that the corporation is dissolved, and that a final franchise tax return has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board. Filing that certificate of dissolution is what causes the corporation's corporate powers, rights, and privileges to cease.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Whenever a corporation has elected to wind up and dissolve a certificate evidencing such election shall forthwith be filed. (b) The certificate shall be an officers’ certificate or shall be signed and verified by at least a majority of the directors then in office or by one or more shareholders authorized to do so by shareholders holding shares representing 50 percent or more of the voting power and shall set forth: (1) That the corporation has elected to wind up and dissolve. (2) If the election was made by the vote of shareholders, the number of shares voting for the election and that the election was made by shareholders representing at least 50 percent of the voting power. (3) If the certificate is executed by a shareholder or shareholders, that the subscribing shareholder or shareholders were authorized to execute the certificate by shareholders holding shares representing at least 50 percent of the voting power. (4) If the election was made by the board pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 1900, the certificate shall also set forth the circumstances showing the corporation to be within one of the categories described in said subdivision. (c) If an election to dissolve made pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 1900 is made by the vote of all the outstanding shares and a statement to that effect is added to the certificate of dissolution pursuant to Section 1905, the separate filing of the certificate of election pursuant to this section is not required."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1901, General Corporation Law, the certificate of election to wind up and dissolve (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1901.)
  "(a) When a corporation has been completely wound up without court proceedings therefor, a majority of the directors then in office shall sign and verify a certificate of dissolution stating:(1) That the corporation has been completely wound up.(2) That its known debts and liabilities have been actually paid, or adequately provided for, or paid or adequately provided for as far as its assets permitted, or that it has incurred no known debts or liabilities, as the case may be. If there are known debts or liabilities for payment of which adequate provision has been made, the certificate shall state what provision has been made, setting forth the name and address of the corporation, person or governmental agency that has assumed or guaranteed the payment, or the name and address of the depositary with which deposit has been made or any other information that may be necessary to enable the creditor or other person to whom payment is to be made to appear and claim payment of the debt or liability.(3) That its known assets have been distributed to the persons entitled thereto or that it acquired no known assets, as the case may be.(4) That the corporation is dissolved.(5) If no certificate of election is to be filed pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 1901, that the election to dissolve was made by the vote of all the outstanding shares.(6) That a final franchise tax return, as described by Section 23332 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board, as required under Part 10.2 (commencing with Section 18401) of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code.(b) The certificate of dissolution shall be filed with the Secretary of State and thereupon the corporate powers, rights, and privileges of the corporation shall cease. The Secretary of State shall notify the Franchise Tax Board of the dissolution."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1905, General Corporation Law, the certificate of dissolution and its effect (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1905.)
  Known gap: This clause corrects a naming trap this research started with: for a California corporation, 'certificate of dissolution' does not refer to the first-filed document the way an analogous name does under the separate LLC dissolution scheme addressed in a different document in this project. For a corporation, the certificate of election under Cal. Corp. Code § 1901 is the (often-skippable) first filing, and the certificate of dissolution under Cal. Corp. Code § 1905 is the filing that actually terminates the corporation's powers, rights, and privileges — the reverse of the LLC scheme, where a certificate of dissolution is filed first and a later certificate of cancellation is what actually ends the LLC's existence. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different filing sequences and document names. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections (§ 1901 and § 1905), not subsections of a single section.

DISTRIBUTION PRIORITY FOR REMAINING CORPORATE ASSETS
After determining that a corporation's known debts and liabilities have all been paid or adequately provided for, state law requires the board to distribute the corporation's remaining assets among the shareholders according to their respective rights and preferences — a formulation that folds in whatever liquidation preferences a corporation's own articles of incorporation may have created among different classes or series of stock — or, if the corporation has no shareholders, to whoever else is entitled to them. If the winding up is happening through a court proceeding, or is subject to court supervision, the distribution cannot be made until after any court-ordered period for creditors to present claims has expired.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "After determining that all the known debts and liabilities of a corporation in the process of winding up have been paid or adequately provided for, the board shall distribute all the remaining corporate assets among the shareholders according to their respective rights and preferences or, if there are no shareholders, to the persons entitled thereto. If the winding up is by court proceeding or subject to court supervision, the distribution shall not be made until after the expiration of any period for the presentation of claims which has been prescribed by order of the court."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2004, General Corporation Law, distribution of remaining assets on winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2004.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different asset-distribution rules. This distribution rule expressly turns on shareholders' 'respective rights and preferences,' which can differ across classes or series of stock under a corporation's own articles of incorporation; this document does not state what those rights and preferences are for any particular corporation, since that is a matter of the corporation's own articles, not something this statute defines on its own. This is a single statutory section (Cal. Corp. Code § 2004); no additional independent source was found for this specific distribution-priority rule.

CONTINUED EXISTENCE AND SURVIVING CLAIMS AFTER DISSOLUTION
Filing the certificate of dissolution does not erase a corporation out of existence for every purpose, and it does not cut off claims against the corporation or its former shareholders. State law lets a dissolved corporation continue to exist afterward, but only for a narrow set of purposes: winding up its affairs, prosecuting or defending lawsuits by or against it in order to collect and discharge what it owes, disposing of and conveying its property, and collecting and dividing its remaining assets — the corporation may not continue conducting business beyond what winding up actually requires. No lawsuit involving the corporation is dismissed just because dissolution happened or because winding-up proceedings are underway, and any asset inadvertently missed during winding up stays with the dissolved corporation for whoever is entitled to it. Separately, state law lets a cause of action against a dissolved corporation — whether it arose before or after the dissolution — be enforced against the dissolved corporation itself, up to its undistributed assets, and, if assets were already distributed to shareholders, against those shareholders individually, up to the lesser of their pro-rata share of the claim or what they actually received on dissolution. A claim against a shareholder on this basis is extinguished unless the claimant sues before the earlier of the ordinary statute of limitations applicable to that claim or four years after the corporation's dissolution became effective.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A corporation which is dissolved nevertheless continues to exist for the purpose of winding up its affairs, prosecuting and defending actions by or against it and enabling it to collect and discharge obligations, dispose of and convey its property and collect and divide its assets, but not for the purpose of continuing business except so far as necessary for the winding up thereof.(b) No action or proceeding to which a corporation is a party abates by the dissolution of the corporation or by reason of proceedings for winding up and dissolution thereof."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2010(a)-(b), General Corporation Law, continued existence for winding-up purposes after dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2010.)
  "Any assets inadvertently or otherwise omitted from the winding up continue in the dissolved corporation for the benefit of the persons entitled thereto upon dissolution of the corporation and on realization shall be distributed accordingly."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2010(c), General Corporation Law, assets omitted from winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2010.)
  "(1) Causes of action against a dissolved corporation, whether arising before or after the dissolution of the corporation, may be enforced against any of the following:(A) Against the dissolved corporation, to the extent of its undistributed assets, including, without limitation, any insurance assets held by the corporation that may be available to satisfy claims.(B) If any of the assets of the dissolved corporation have been distributed to shareholders, against shareholders of the dissolved corporation to the extent of their pro rata share of the claim or to the extent of the corporate assets distributed to them upon dissolution of the corporation, whichever is less.A shareholder’s total liability under this section may not exceed the total amount of assets of the dissolved corporation distributed to the shareholder upon dissolution of the corporation.(2) Except as set forth in subdivision (c), all causes of action against a shareholder of a dissolved corporation arising under this section are extinguished unless the claimant commences a proceeding to enforce the cause of action against that shareholder of a dissolved corporation prior to the earlier of the following:(A) The expiration of the statute of limitations applicable to the cause of action.(B) Four years after the effective date of the dissolution of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2011(a)(1)-(2), General Corporation Law, causes of action against a dissolved corporation and its shareholders, and the four-year cutoff (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2011.)

The first two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2010, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones; the third quote is a different section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2011, addressed separately. This document states only the general rule under section 2011(a)(1)-(2) — enforcement against the corporation's undistributed assets or against shareholders individually, and the four-year/statute-of-limitations cutoff; it does not address the separate quiet-title-action survival rule in section 2011(c) (which the statute states has no time limit), the procedural rule allowing suit against shareholders in the corporation's own name under section 2011(a)(3), or the corporation's or creditors' separate rights under Corporations Code section 2009 or the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, which section 2011(a)(3) expressly preserves without this document independently verifying their content.

FRANCHISE TAX BOARD CLEARANCE AND THE MINIMUM FRANCHISE TAX
Filing a certificate of dissolution does not, by itself, stop the corporation's minimum franchise tax. Under California's Revenue and Taxation Code, a corporation owes no further minimum franchise tax for a given taxable year only if it does all of the following: files a timely final franchise tax return with the Franchise Tax Board for that taxable year; does no further business in California after that taxable year ends; and files a certificate of dissolution with the Secretary of State within 12 months of the date that final return was filed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(1) A corporation shall not be subject to the minimum franchise tax imposed by this chapter for a taxable year if the corporation does all of the following:(A) Files a timely final franchise tax return for a taxable year with the Franchise Tax Board.(B) Does not do business in this state after the end of the taxable year for which the final franchise tax return was filed.(C) (i) In the case of a corporation other than a corporation described in clause (ii), files a certificate of dissolution or surrender with the Secretary of State, in accordance with Sections 1809, 1905, 2112, 6615, 8615, and 12635 of the Corporations Code and Section 3126 of the Financial Code, before the end of the 12-month period beginning with the date the final franchise tax return was filed."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c), Corporation Franchise Tax, relief from the minimum franchise tax on timely final return and dissolution filing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23332.)
  Known gap: This confirms, with a correction, the research assumption that a distinct Franchise Tax Board tax-clearance mechanism applies to corporations. Verified directly, that mechanism is Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c), not Corp. Code § 1905 itself: section 1905(a)(6), addressed elsewhere in this document, only requires the corporation's own certificate of dissolution to represent that a final franchise tax return has been or will be filed — it is section 23332(c), a separate statute, that actually ties minimum-franchise-tax relief to that representation being true and to the certificate of dissolution being filed within 12 months of the final return. This mechanism mirrors, but is not the same statute as, the analogous LLC mechanism verified elsewhere in this project's LLC Dissolution and Cancellation document: corporations look to Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332, while LLCs look to a different section, Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not tax advice about any particular corporation's own filings or filing deadlines. This document does not independently verify Rev. & Tax. Code § 18601 (defining a 'final franchise tax return') or the several other entity-specific dissolution and surrender statutes that section 23332(c)(1)(C) cross-references by number (Corp. Code §§ 1809, 2112, 6615, 8615, and 12635, and Fin. Code § 3126) beyond the fact that section 23332 itself names them; their own text was not independently fetched and verified as part of this research. This is a single statutory section (Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c)); no additional independent source was found for this specific tax-clearance mechanism.

DISSOLUTION DECLARATION AND SIGNATURES
The undersigned, being a majority of the directors of Acme, Inc. then in office, declare the following: Acme, Inc. has been completely wound up; Acme, Inc.'s known debts and liabilities have been actually paid, or adequately provided for, or paid or adequately provided for as far as its assets permitted, or Acme, Inc. incurred no known debts or liabilities; Acme, Inc.'s known assets have been distributed to the persons entitled to them, or Acme, Inc. acquired no known assets; and a final franchise tax return for Acme, Inc. has been or will be filed with the California Franchise Tax Board.

☐ The election to dissolve Acme, Inc. was made by the vote of all the outstanding shares, and this statement satisfies the requirement to include it in the certificate of dissolution, so that no separate certificate of election need be filed.
☐ The election to dissolve Acme, Inc. was not made by the vote of all the outstanding shares, and a certificate of election has been or will be filed separately.

Acme, Inc. is dissolved.

Signed:

_______________________________ Date: _______________
_______________________________ Date: _______________
(Add additional signature lines as needed for a majority of the directors then in office.)

expectedJSON.body: Formally dissolving a California corporation generally involves a certificate evidencing the election to wind up and dissolve, filed once that election is made, and a separate certificate of dissolution filed later, once winding up is complete. The certificate of election must be an officers' certificate, or be signed and verified by a majority of the sitting directors, or by shareholders authorized to sign it by holders of 50 percent or more of the voting power, and it must state that the corporation elected to dissolve along with details of how that election was made. If the election was made by the vote of all the outstanding shares — not merely 50 percent or more — and the later certificate of dissolution itself states that the election was made by all outstanding shares, the separate certificate of election does not need to be filed at all. The certificate of dissolution itself, once winding up is complete, is signed and verified by a majority of the sitting directors and states that the corporation has been completely wound up, how its known debts and liabilities were handled, that its known assets have been distributed (or that none were acquired), that the corporation is dissolved, and that a final franchise tax return has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board. Filing that certificate of dissolution is what causes the corporation's corporate powers, rights, and privileges to cease.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, the certificate of election to wind up and dissolve
citations.quote: (a) Whenever a corporation has elected to wind up and dissolve a certificate evidencing such election shall forthwith be filed. (b) The certificate shall be an officers’ certificate or shall be signed and verified by at least a majority of the directors then in office or by one or more shareholders authorized to do so by shareholders holding shares representing 50 percent or more of the voting power and shall set forth: (1) That the corporation has elected to wind up and dissolve. (2) If the election was made by the vote of shareholders, the number of shares voting for the election and that the election was made by shareholders representing at least 50 percent of the voting power. (3) If the certificate is executed by a shareholder or shareholders, that the subscribing shareholder or shareholders were authorized to execute the certificate by shareholders holding shares representing at least 50 percent of the voting power. (4) If the election was made by the board pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 1900, the certificate shall also set forth the circumstances showing the corporation to be within one of the categories described in said subdivision. (c) If an election to dissolve made pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 1900 is made by the vote of all the outstanding shares and a statement to that effect is added to the certificate of dissolution pursuant to Section 1905, the separate filing of the certificate of election pursuant to this section is not required.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, the certificate of dissolution and its effect
citations.quote: (a) When a corporation has been completely wound up without court proceedings therefor, a majority of the directors then in office shall sign and verify a certificate of dissolution stating:(1) That the corporation has been completely wound up.(2) That its known debts and liabilities have been actually paid, or adequately provided for, or paid or adequately provided for as far as its assets permitted, or that it has incurred no known debts or liabilities, as the case may be. If there are known debts or liabilities for payment of which adequate provision has been made, the certificate shall state what provision has been made, setting forth the name and address of the corporation, person or governmental agency that has assumed or guaranteed the payment, or the name and address of the depositary with which deposit has been made or any other information that may be necessary to enable the creditor or other person to whom payment is to be made to appear and claim payment of the debt or liability.(3) That its known assets have been distributed to the persons entitled thereto or that it acquired no known assets, as the case may be.(4) That the corporation is dissolved.(5) If no certificate of election is to be filed pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 1901, that the election to dissolve was made by the vote of all the outstanding shares.(6) That a final franchise tax return, as described by Section 23332 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board, as required under Part 10.2 (commencing with Section 18401) of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code.(b) The certificate of dissolution shall be filed with the Secretary of State and thereupon the corporate powers, rights, and privileges of the corporation shall cease. The Secretary of State shall notify the Franchise Tax Board of the dissolution.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause corrects a naming trap this research started with: for a California corporation, 'certificate of dissolution' does not refer to the first-filed document the way an analogous name does under the separate LLC dissolution scheme addressed in a different document in this project. For a corporation, the certificate of election under Cal. Corp. Code § 1901 is the (often-skippable) first filing, and the certificate of dissolution under Cal. Corp. Code § 1905 is the filing that actually terminates the corporation's powers, rights, and privileges — the reverse of the LLC scheme, where a certificate of dissolution is filed first and a later certificate of cancellation is what actually ends the LLC's existence. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different filing sequences and document names. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections (§ 1901 and § 1905), not subsections of a single section.

expectedJSON.body: After determining that a corporation's known debts and liabilities have all been paid or adequately provided for, state law requires the board to distribute the corporation's remaining assets among the shareholders according to their respective rights and preferences — a formulation that folds in whatever liquidation preferences a corporation's own articles of incorporation may have created among different classes or series of stock — or, if the corporation has no shareholders, to whoever else is entitled to them. If the winding up is happening through a court proceeding, or is subject to court supervision, the distribution cannot be made until after any court-ordered period for creditors to present claims has expired.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, distribution of remaining assets on winding up
citations.quote: After determining that all the known debts and liabilities of a corporation in the process of winding up have been paid or adequately provided for, the board shall distribute all the remaining corporate assets among the shareholders according to their respective rights and preferences or, if there are no shareholders, to the persons entitled thereto. If the winding up is by court proceeding or subject to court supervision, the distribution shall not be made until after the expiration of any period for the presentation of claims which has been prescribed by order of the court.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different asset-distribution rules. This distribution rule expressly turns on shareholders' 'respective rights and preferences,' which can differ across classes or series of stock under a corporation's own articles of incorporation; this document does not state what those rights and preferences are for any particular corporation, since that is a matter of the corporation's own articles, not something this statute defines on its own. This is a single statutory section (Cal. Corp. Code § 2004); no additional independent source was found for this specific distribution-priority rule.

expectedJSON.body: Filing the certificate of dissolution does not erase a corporation out of existence for every purpose, and it does not cut off claims against the corporation or its former shareholders. State law lets a dissolved corporation continue to exist afterward, but only for a narrow set of purposes: winding up its affairs, prosecuting or defending lawsuits by or against it in order to collect and discharge what it owes, disposing of and conveying its property, and collecting and dividing its remaining assets — the corporation may not continue conducting business beyond what winding up actually requires. No lawsuit involving the corporation is dismissed just because dissolution happened or because winding-up proceedings are underway, and any asset inadvertently missed during winding up stays with the dissolved corporation for whoever is entitled to it. Separately, state law lets a cause of action against a dissolved corporation — whether it arose before or after the dissolution — be enforced against the dissolved corporation itself, up to its undistributed assets, and, if assets were already distributed to shareholders, against those shareholders individually, up to the lesser of their pro-rata share of the claim or what they actually received on dissolution. A claim against a shareholder on this basis is extinguished unless the claimant sues before the earlier of the ordinary statute of limitations applicable to that claim or four years after the corporation's dissolution became effective.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, continued existence for winding-up purposes after dissolution
citations.quote: (a) A corporation which is dissolved nevertheless continues to exist for the purpose of winding up its affairs, prosecuting and defending actions by or against it and enabling it to collect and discharge obligations, dispose of and convey its property and collect and divide its assets, but not for the purpose of continuing business except so far as necessary for the winding up thereof.(b) No action or proceeding to which a corporation is a party abates by the dissolution of the corporation or by reason of proceedings for winding up and dissolution thereof.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, assets omitted from winding up
citations.quote: Any assets inadvertently or otherwise omitted from the winding up continue in the dissolved corporation for the benefit of the persons entitled thereto upon dissolution of the corporation and on realization shall be distributed accordingly.

citations.cite: General Corporation Law, causes of action against a dissolved corporation and its shareholders, and the four-year cutoff
citations.quote: (1) Causes of action against a dissolved corporation, whether arising before or after the dissolution of the corporation, may be enforced against any of the following:(A) Against the dissolved corporation, to the extent of its undistributed assets, including, without limitation, any insurance assets held by the corporation that may be available to satisfy claims.(B) If any of the assets of the dissolved corporation have been distributed to shareholders, against shareholders of the dissolved corporation to the extent of their pro rata share of the claim or to the extent of the corporate assets distributed to them upon dissolution of the corporation, whichever is less.A shareholder’s total liability under this section may not exceed the total amount of assets of the dissolved corporation distributed to the shareholder upon dissolution of the corporation.(2) Except as set forth in subdivision (c), all causes of action against a shareholder of a dissolved corporation arising under this section are extinguished unless the claimant commences a proceeding to enforce the cause of action against that shareholder of a dissolved corporation prior to the earlier of the following:(A) The expiration of the statute of limitations applicable to the cause of action.(B) Four years after the effective date of the dissolution of the corporation.

The first two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2010, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones; the third quote is a different section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2011, addressed separately. This document states only the general rule under section 2011(a)(1)-(2) — enforcement against the corporation's undistributed assets or against shareholders individually, and the four-year/statute-of-limitations cutoff; it does not address the separate quiet-title-action survival rule in section 2011(c) (which the statute states has no time limit), the procedural rule allowing suit against shareholders in the corporation's own name under section 2011(a)(3), or the corporation's or creditors' separate rights under Corporations Code section 2009 or the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, which section 2011(a)(3) expressly preserves without this document independently verifying their content.

expectedJSON.body: Filing a certificate of dissolution does not, by itself, stop the corporation's minimum franchise tax. Under California's Revenue and Taxation Code, a corporation owes no further minimum franchise tax for a given taxable year only if it does all of the following: files a timely final franchise tax return with the Franchise Tax Board for that taxable year; does no further business in California after that taxable year ends; and files a certificate of dissolution with the Secretary of State within 12 months of the date that final return was filed.

citations.cite: Corporation Franchise Tax, relief from the minimum franchise tax on timely final return and dissolution filing
citations.quote: (1) A corporation shall not be subject to the minimum franchise tax imposed by this chapter for a taxable year if the corporation does all of the following:(A) Files a timely final franchise tax return for a taxable year with the Franchise Tax Board.(B) Does not do business in this state after the end of the taxable year for which the final franchise tax return was filed.(C) (i) In the case of a corporation other than a corporation described in clause (ii), files a certificate of dissolution or surrender with the Secretary of State, in accordance with Sections 1809, 1905, 2112, 6615, 8615, and 12635 of the Corporations Code and Section 3126 of the Financial Code, before the end of the 12-month period beginning with the date the final franchise tax return was filed.

expectedJSON.gap: This confirms, with a correction, the research assumption that a distinct Franchise Tax Board tax-clearance mechanism applies to corporations. Verified directly, that mechanism is Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c), not Corp. Code § 1905 itself: section 1905(a)(6), addressed elsewhere in this document, only requires the corporation's own certificate of dissolution to represent that a final franchise tax return has been or will be filed — it is section 23332(c), a separate statute, that actually ties minimum-franchise-tax relief to that representation being true and to the certificate of dissolution being filed within 12 months of the final return. This mechanism mirrors, but is not the same statute as, the analogous LLC mechanism verified elsewhere in this project's LLC Dissolution and Cancellation document: corporations look to Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332, while LLCs look to a different section, Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not tax advice about any particular corporation's own filings or filing deadlines. This document does not independently verify Rev. & Tax. Code § 18601 (defining a 'final franchise tax return') or the several other entity-specific dissolution and surrender statutes that section 23332(c)(1)(C) cross-references by number (Corp. Code §§ 1809, 2112, 6615, 8615, and 12635, and Fin. Code § 3126) beyond the fact that section 23332 itself names them; their own text was not independently fetched and verified as part of this research. This is a single statutory section (Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c)); no additional independent source was found for this specific tax-clearance mechanism.
